articles.title: The Silk Road
articles.body:
The Silk Road was never a single road, nor was it used only for silk. It was a shifting web of routes that linked China to the Mediterranean, crossing deserts, mountains, and the territories of many peoples.

Goods certainly moved along it — silk travelling west, but also glass, spices, and horses in many directions. Yet historians increasingly stress that ideas travelled just as far. Religions, technologies, and artistic styles spread between distant cultures, carried by the very merchants who carried cloth.

The network declined as sea routes grew cheaper and safer from the fifteenth century onward. Even so, its lasting importance lies less in the trade itself than in what that trade made possible: sustained contact between civilisations that might otherwise have remained strangers.

articles.title: The Surprising Journey of Coffee
articles.body:
Few drinks have shaped daily life as quietly as coffee. According to a popular legend, its energising effect was first noticed by an Ethiopian goat herder who saw his animals grow lively after eating the bright red berries of a certain shrub. Whether or not the story is true, by the fifteenth century coffee was being roasted and brewed in the Arabian Peninsula, where it became central to social and religious life.

From there the drink spread along trade routes to the great cities of the Ottoman world. Coffee houses, sometimes called 'schools of the wise', became places where people gathered to talk, play games, listen to music, and argue about the news. Rulers were not always pleased; on several occasions the authorities tried to close these establishments, fearing that lively conversation might turn into criticism of those in power.

When coffee reached Europe in the seventeenth century, it met a similar mixture of enthusiasm and suspicion. Yet the coffee house soon took on the same role it had played further east, drawing merchants, writers, and scientists into long discussions. Some historians argue that these crowded, smoky rooms helped spread the new ideas of the age more effectively than any library could.

Today coffee is grown across a wide band of tropical countries and consumed almost everywhere. The legend of the dancing goats may be impossible to prove, but the drink's deeper history is clear enough: wherever it has travelled, coffee has done more than wake people up. It has given them a reason to sit down together.

articles.title: How Clever Is an Octopus?
articles.body:
For an animal with no bones and a lifespan of only a year or two, the octopus is astonishingly clever. Its body contains around five hundred million nerve cells, but, remarkably, most of them are not in its brain. They are spread through its eight arms, each of which can taste, touch, and even make simple decisions on its own. In a sense, an octopus thinks not only with its head but with its whole body.

This distributed intelligence allows octopuses to perform feats that surprise the scientists who study them. In laboratories they have learned to open jars to reach food, to recognise individual human faces, and to find their way through mazes. Some have been filmed carrying coconut shells across the sea floor, fitting them together later as portable shelters — a clear example of using tools.

Perhaps their most famous skill is disguise. Special cells in their skin let them change colour, and even texture, in less than a second, melting into rock, sand, or coral. Curiously, octopuses appear to be colour-blind, which makes their ability to match their surroundings so precisely all the more puzzling.

Because they are so different from us — and from almost every other intelligent creature — octopuses raise a fascinating question. Intelligence, it seems, is not a single ladder with humans at the top. It may instead be something that nature has invented more than once, in forms we are only beginning to understand.

items.en: What is surprising is that most of its nerve cells are not in the brain but in the arms.

articles.title: The Power of the Placebo
articles.body:
Imagine being given a pill that contains no active medicine at all — just sugar — and yet feeling genuinely better afterwards. This puzzling effect, known as the placebo response, has been recorded for centuries and continues to challenge our understanding of the mind and body.

In carefully designed trials, some patients receive the real drug while others unknowingly receive a dummy version. Researchers expect the dummy group to show no improvement, yet these patients often do improve, reporting less pain, better sleep, or reduced anxiety. The effect tends to be strongest for symptoms closely tied to perception, and weakest for measurable physical changes such as the shrinking of a tumour.

What could explain this? Part of the answer seems to lie in expectation. When we believe a treatment will work, the brain may release its own pain-relieving chemicals, and the simple ritual of being cared for can itself reduce stress. Intriguingly, the placebo effect can persist even when patients are openly told that they are taking a dummy pill, which suggests that conscious belief is not the whole story.

Far from being a mere nuisance to be subtracted from trial results, the placebo response is increasingly studied as a genuine biological phenomenon. Understanding it better could help doctors make real treatments more effective, by paying closer attention to something medicine has long underestimated: the powerful influence of the mind upon the body.

articles.title: Who Really Built the Pyramids?
articles.body:
For a long time, popular imagination pictured the Egyptian pyramids as the work of vast armies of slaves, driven by the whip beneath a burning sun. This dramatic image, repeated in countless films, turns out to be largely a myth. The evidence uncovered by archaeologists tells a rather different story.

Near the pyramids of Giza, excavations have revealed the remains of a well-organised workers' town, complete with bakeries, breweries, and areas for preparing fish and meat. The sheer quantity of food suggests that the labourers were fed well — hardly the treatment one would expect for slaves. Skeletons found in nearby cemeteries show signs of hard physical labour, but also of medical care, with broken bones that had been carefully set and allowed to heal.

Most scholars now believe that the pyramids were built largely by paid workers and seasonal labourers, many of them ordinary farmers. During the months when the Nile flooded their fields, farming was impossible, and the building projects offered employment, food, and perhaps a sense of shared purpose. Skilled craftsmen lived on the site all year round, while teams of workers rotated in and out.

The truth, then, is in some ways more impressive than the myth. The pyramids stand not as monuments to cruelty alone, but as evidence of a society able to organise, feed, and motivate thousands of people toward a single enormous goal.

articles.title: What Causes the Northern Lights?
articles.body:
On clear nights in the far north, the sky sometimes fills with waves of green, pink, and violet light. These glowing curtains are called the Northern Lights, or the aurora. For hundreds of years, people told stories to explain them. Some believed the lights were the spirits of the dead; others thought they were a warning of coming danger.

Today we understand what really causes the aurora. It begins with the Sun, which constantly sends out a stream of tiny particles into space. When these particles reach the Earth, most of them are pushed away by our planet's magnetic field. But near the North and South Poles, some particles slip through and crash into the gases high in our atmosphere.

When the particles hit these gases, they make them glow, rather like the gas inside a neon sign. The colour depends on which gas is struck and how high up it is. Oxygen usually produces green or red light, while nitrogen can create blue or purple. The same thing happens near the South Pole, where the display is known as the Southern Lights.

The best time to see the aurora is on a dark, cloudless night, far from city lights. Many travellers now journey to countries such as Norway, Iceland, and Canada just for the chance to watch the sky come alive. For most of them, it is a sight they never forget.

items.q: What did some people in the past believe about the lights?
opts: That they were the spirits of the dead
That they were caused by the Sun
That they were made by neon signs
That they came from city lights
items.tr: Geçmişte bazı insanlar ışıkların ölülerin ruhları olduğuna inanıyordu.
items.en: Some people once believed the lights were the spirits of the dead.

items.q: Where do the particles from the Sun manage to enter the atmosphere?
opts: Near the North and South Poles
items.tr: Güneş'ten gelen parçacıklar atmosfere Kuzey ve Güney Kutupları yakınında girer.
items.en: The particles slip through near the North and South Poles.

items.q: What decides the colour of the aurora?
opts: Which gas is hit and how high it is
items.tr: Auroranın rengi, hangi gazın ve hangi yükseklikte vurulduğuna bağlıdır.
items.en: The colour depends on which gas is struck and at what height.

items.q: Why does the writer compare the glowing gas to a neon sign?
opts: To show the gas is dangerous
To prove neon signs are natural
To help explain how the gas lights up
items.tr: Yazar, gazın nasıl ışıdığını açıklamaya yardımcı olmak için neon tabelaya benzetir.
items.en: The comparison helps explain how the gas glows.

opts: A dark, cloudless night away from city lights
A bright, cloudy night in a city
items.tr: Aurorayı görmek için en iyi koşul, şehir ışıklarından uzak, karanlık ve bulutsuz bir gecedir.
items.en: The best condition is a dark, cloudless night far from city lights.

articles.title: Why Do We Laugh?
articles.body:
Laughter seems simple, but scientists still find it surprising. We often think we laugh because something is funny, yet most laughter has little to do with jokes. Studies of ordinary conversations show that people usually laugh at quite plain comments, such as 'I'll see you later' or 'It was nice to meet you'. We laugh, it seems, mainly to connect with other people.

Laughter is social in another way too. We are far more likely to laugh when we are with others than when we are alone. A funny film might make you smile by yourself, but the same film can make a whole cinema roar together. In this sense, laughter works like a kind of glue, helping a group feel close and relaxed.

There may be health benefits as well. When we laugh, our muscles relax, we breathe more deeply, and the body releases chemicals that make us feel good. Some doctors believe that regular laughter can lower stress and may even be good for the heart, although more research is still needed.

Babies begin to laugh long before they can speak, and people laugh in every culture on Earth. This suggests that laughter is not something we simply learn, but a deep part of being human — a signal, older than language, that says we feel safe and we belong.

items.q: What do studies of conversations show about laughter?
opts: People only laugh at good jokes
People often laugh at quite ordinary comments
items.tr: Çalışmalar, insanların çoğu zaman oldukça sıradan sözlere güldüğünü gösterir.
items.en: Studies show people often laugh at quite ordinary comments, not just jokes.

items.q: When are we most likely to laugh?
opts: When we are with other people
items.tr: Başkalarıyla birlikteyken gülme olasılığımız çok daha yüksektir.
items.en: We are far more likely to laugh when we are with others.

items.q: Why does the writer compare laughter to 'glue'?
opts: Because it is hard to remove
Because it is used in films
Because it helps groups feel close
items.tr: Yazar, gülmenin grupları yakınlaştırdığı için onu tutkala benzetir.
items.en: The comparison shows laughter helps a group feel close and connected.

opts: It is a deep, natural part of being human

It is different in every country
items.tr: Bebek örneği, gülmenin insan olmanın derin ve doğal bir parçası olduğunu gösterir.
items.en: The example of babies suggests laughter is a deep, natural part of being human.

articles.title: The City That Fights the Sea
articles.body:
Few cities are as instantly recognisable as Venice, with its canals, bridges, and palaces rising directly out of the water. Yet the very setting that makes the city so beautiful also threatens its survival. Built on wooden posts driven into the mud of a shallow lagoon more than a thousand years ago, Venice has always lived in an uneasy relationship with the sea.

The problem has grown worse in recent times. The ground beneath the city has slowly sunk, partly because of the natural settling of the soil and partly because of water once pumped from below for industry. At the same time, global sea levels have been rising. As a result, the high tides that flood the famous Saint Mark's Square now arrive more often, and reach higher, than they did a century ago.

In response, engineers have built an enormous system of movable barriers at the entrances to the lagoon. When a dangerous tide is forecast, the barriers rise from the seabed to hold back the water. The system has already prevented serious flooding on several occasions, yet many experts warn that it cannot be a permanent answer if the seas keep rising.

Venice has thus become a symbol far beyond Italy. Its struggle raises a question that more and more coastal cities will soon have to face: how do you protect an irreplaceable place from a danger that is slow, steady, and steadily growing?

items.q: Why is Venice's beautiful setting also a threat?
opts: The canals are too narrow for boats
The city sits in water and is vulnerable to the sea
items.tr: Venedik suyun içinde kurulu olduğundan denize karşı savunmasızdır; bu yüzden güzelliği aynı zamanda tehdittir.
items.en: Because Venice sits in the water, it is vulnerable to the sea that makes it beautiful.

items.q: What are the two main reasons flooding has got worse?
opts: The land sinking and sea levels rising
items.tr: Sular, zeminin çökmesi ve deniz seviyesinin yükselmesi nedeniyle daha kötü basıyor.
items.en: Flooding has worsened because the land has sunk and sea levels have risen.

items.q: How do the movable barriers protect the city?

They rise from the seabed to hold back dangerous tides

items.en: The barriers rise from the seabed to hold back dangerous tides.

opts: They may not work if the seas keep rising

opts: It is the oldest city in the world

items.en: Its struggle mirrors a danger that many coastal cities will soon confront.

articles.title: Why People Live Near Volcanoes
articles.body:
It might seem foolish to build a home in the shadow of a volcano, yet millions of people around the world do exactly that. For them, the danger of a future eruption is outweighed by advantages that are present every single day.

The most important of these is the soil. When a volcano erupts, the ash and lava it produces are rich in minerals such as potassium and phosphorus. Over many years, this material breaks down into some of the most fertile land on the planet. Farmers on the slopes of volcanoes can often grow crops that would be difficult elsewhere, from coffee and grapes to rice and vegetables.

Volcanic regions offer other resources too. In several countries, the heat stored beneath the ground is used to generate clean electricity and to warm homes, a technology known as geothermal energy. Volcanoes also attract tourists, whose spending supports local businesses, and they often contain valuable minerals that can be mined.

Scientists, meanwhile, work hard to reduce the risks. By monitoring small earthquakes, escaping gases, and tiny changes in the shape of the ground, they can often warn communities before an eruption begins. The relationship between people and volcanoes is therefore not simply one of fear. It is a long-standing bargain, in which communities accept a rare but serious threat in exchange for benefits they depend on throughout their lives.

items.q: According to the text, why do people accept the risk of living near volcanoes?
opts: They do not know the volcano is active
The daily benefits outweigh the rare danger
The government forces them to stay
items.tr: İnsanlar, her gün var olan yararlar nadir tehlikeden ağır bastığı için riski kabul eder.
items.en: People accept the risk because the everyday benefits outweigh the rare danger.

items.q: Why is volcanic soil so valuable to farmers?
opts: It is found only near cities
Ash and lava make it rich in minerals
items.tr: Kül ve lav toprağı minerallerce zengin yaptığı için volkanik toprak çok değerlidir.
items.en: Ash and lava make the soil rich in minerals, so it is highly fertile.

opts: Clean power and heat from the heat beneath the ground
items.tr: Jeotermal enerji, yer altındaki ısıdan elde edilen temiz elektrik ve ısıtmadır.
items.en: Geothermal energy is clean power and heating drawn from the heat beneath the ground.

opts: By watching for warning signs before an eruption
By banning farming on the slopes

items.en: Scientists reduce danger by monitoring warning signs before an eruption.

opts: People pay money to the volcano

items.tr: 'Pazarlık' ifadesi, toplulukların değerli yararlar karşılığında ciddi bir riski kabul etmesini anlatır.
items.en: The 'bargain' means communities accept a serious risk in exchange for valuable benefits.

articles.title: When a Language Falls Silent
articles.body:
Of the roughly seven thousand languages spoken today, experts believe that nearly half may disappear before the end of this century. A language is usually considered safe only while children are still learning it at home. Once parents begin to raise their children in a more powerful national language instead, the older tongue can vanish within a single generation.

Why should this matter? Each language is far more than a list of words. It carries a unique way of describing the world, along with stories, songs, and knowledge built up over centuries. When the last fluent speaker of a language dies, much of that knowledge dies too, and it can almost never be fully recovered.

Around the world, communities are now fighting to keep their languages alive. Some record their elders so that future generations can hear how words were spoken. Others create schools where lessons are taught in the local tongue, or build apps and dictionaries to help young learners. These efforts do not always succeed, but they show a growing awareness of what is at stake.

Protecting a language is difficult and slow work, and it cannot be done by outsiders alone. In the end, a language survives only if its own community chooses to speak it. Yet the wider world can help, by treating small languages not as obstacles to progress but as treasures worth keeping.

items.q: According to the text, when is a language usually considered safe?
opts: While children are still learning it at home
When it has a written dictionary
When it is taught to outsiders
items.tr: Bir dil, çocuklar onu evde öğrenmeye devam ettiği sürece güvende sayılır.
items.en: A language is considered safe while children are still learning it at home.

items.q: Why does the writer say losing a language matters?
opts: It carries unique knowledge that can rarely be recovered
It lowers the value of dictionaries
items.tr: Her dil, neredeyse geri kazanılamayan özgün bilgi taşıdığı için kaybı önemlidir.
items.en: A language carries unique knowledge that can almost never be recovered.

items.q: What is one method communities use to protect their languages?
opts: Recording elders and creating local-language schools
items.tr: Topluluklar, yaşlıları kaydetmek ve yerel dilde okullar kurmak gibi yöntemler kullanır.
items.en: Communities record elders and create schools that teach in the local language.

opts: That its own community chooses to speak it
items.tr: Bir dil ancak kendi topluluğu onu konuşmayı seçerse hayatta kalır.
items.en: A language survives only if its own community chooses to speak it.

items.q: What is the writer's overall attitude towards small languages?
items.tr: Yazar küçük dilleri korunmaya değer hazineler olarak görür.
items.en: The writer regards small languages as treasures worth keeping.

articles.title: The Dancing Language of Bees
articles.body:
When a honeybee finds a rich patch of flowers, it faces a problem: how can it tell the rest of the hive where the food is? Bees cannot speak, and the inside of a hive is completely dark. Yet somehow a single bee can send hundreds of others straight to a meal that may be kilometres away.

The answer, discovered by a curious scientist almost a century ago, is a kind of dance. Back at the hive, the successful bee moves in a tight figure-of-eight pattern, shaking its body as it goes. The direction of this 'waggle' tells the other bees which way to fly in relation to the sun, while the length of the dance signals how far they must travel.

What makes this so remarkable is that the bees are communicating abstract information, not simply reacting to what is in front of them. A dancing bee is, in effect, describing a place that the others cannot see. For a long time, many people assumed that such behaviour was unique to humans.

Scientists are still studying exactly how the watching bees read the dance in the dark, perhaps by feeling its movements and listening to tiny sounds. Whatever the full explanation, the discovery changed the way we think about animal minds, reminding us that intelligence in nature can take forms we never expected.

items.q: What problem does a honeybee face after finding flowers?
opts: It cannot fly back to the hive
It must tell other bees where the food is without speaking
It cannot eat the food alone
items.tr: Arı, konuşmadan diğerlerine yiyeceğin yerini anlatmak zorundadır.
items.en: The bee must tell others where the food is without being able to speak.

items.q: What does the direction of the waggle dance tell other bees?
opts: Which way to fly in relation to the sun
items.tr: 'Waggle' dansının yönü, güneşe göre hangi yöne uçacaklarını gösterir.
items.en: The direction of the waggle shows which way to fly relative to the sun.

items.q: Why does the writer find the dance so remarkable?
opts: It is very beautiful to watch
It uses no movement at all
The bees communicate about a place they cannot see

items.en: The bees communicate abstract information about a place they cannot see.

items.q: What was once widely assumed about this kind of behaviour?
opts: That it was unique to humans
That only birds could do it

items.en: It was long assumed that such behaviour was unique to humans.

items.q: What does the discovery suggest about intelligence in nature?
opts: It exists only in large animals
It can take forms we never expected
It is the same in every species
items.tr: Keşif, doğadaki zekânın beklemediğimiz biçimler alabileceğini gösterir.
items.en: It suggests intelligence in nature can take forms we never expected.

articles.title: The Oldest Way to Make Bread
articles.body:
Long before anyone sold packets of yeast in shops, people made bread rise using something much simpler: a mixture of flour and water left out in the open air. This mixture, known as a sourdough starter, catches tiny living things called wild yeast and friendly bacteria that float all around us.

Left for a few days and fed with fresh flour, the starter begins to bubble and grow. When a baker mixes some of it into dough, these tiny organisms produce gas, and that gas makes the bread rise. They also create the slightly sour taste that gives this kind of bread its name.

Making sourdough takes patience. The starter must be fed regularly, almost like a small pet, and the bread itself needs many hours to rise. For this reason, many people gave it up when faster methods appeared. In recent years, however, sourdough has become popular again, partly because people enjoy making things slowly with their own hands.

There may be health reasons too. Some studies suggest that the long, slow rise makes the bread easier for the body to digest. Whether or not that is true, sourdough connects us to one of the oldest skills in human history, a skill that needs nothing more than flour, water, time, and a little care.

opts: Flour and water left in the open air
items.tr: Ekşi maya başlangıcı, açık havada bırakılan un ve sudan yapılır.
items.en: A sourdough starter is made from flour and water left in the open air.

items.q: What makes sourdough bread rise?
opts: Gas produced by tiny living organisms
items.tr: Ekşi maya ekmeğini, minik canlıların ürettiği gaz kabartır.
items.en: Gas produced by the tiny living organisms makes the bread rise.

items.tr: Daha hızlı yöntemler çıkınca birçok kişi ekşi mayayı bıraktı.
items.en: Many people gave it up when faster methods appeared.

opts: People enjoy making things slowly by hand
items.tr: İnsanlar bir şeyi yavaşça elleriyle yapmaktan keyif aldığı için ekşi maya yeniden popüler oldu.
items.en: It is popular again partly because people enjoy making things slowly by hand.

opts: The slow rise may make it easier to digest
It removes the need for vegetables
items.tr: Metin, yavaş kabarmanın ekmeği sindirmesi daha kolay hale getirebileceğinden söz eder.
items.en: The text mentions the slow rise may make the bread easier to digest.

articles.title: How the Clock Changed the World
articles.body:
For most of human history, people measured time by the sun, the seasons, and the natural rhythms of the body. A task took as long as it took, and few people needed to know the exact hour. The mechanical clock, which spread through Europe from the medieval period onward, slowly and quietly transformed this way of life.

At first, clocks were enormous machines housed in church and town towers, ringing bells to mark the hours for everyone within hearing. As they became smaller and cheaper, they moved into homes and, eventually, into pockets. With them came a new idea: that time was something fixed and divisible, the same for everyone, to be measured and not merely felt.

This change had effects that reached far beyond convenience. Factories could now demand that workers arrive at a precise minute and labour for an exact number of hours. Trains could run to shared timetables, and business could be coordinated across great distances. In countless ways, the clock made the modern, tightly organised world possible.

Yet some thinkers argue that we paid a price for this precision. By turning time into something to be counted and saved, we may have made ourselves its servants, forever rushing and forever short of it. The clock gave us extraordinary order, but it also taught us, perhaps too well, to feel that time is always running out.

items.q: How did most people measure time before mechanical clocks?
opts: By the sun, seasons, and natural rhythms
items.tr: İnsanlar çoğunlukla zamanı güneş, mevsimler ve doğal ritimlerle ölçerdi.
items.en: Most people measured time by the sun, the seasons, and natural rhythms.

items.q: What new idea about time did clocks bring?
opts: That time was fixed, divisible, and the same for everyone
That time could be felt but not measured
items.tr: Saatler, zamanın sabit, bölünebilir ve herkes için aynı olduğu fikrini getirdi.
items.en: Clocks brought the idea that time was fixed, divisible, and the same for everyone.

items.q: What does the writer say clocks made possible?
items.tr: Yazara göre saatler modern, sıkı örgütlenmiş dünyayı mümkün kıldı.
items.en: The writer says clocks made the modern, tightly organised world possible.

items.q: What 'price' do some thinkers say we paid?
opts: We forgot how to build towers
We became servants of time, always rushing
items.tr: Bazı düşünürlere göre, sürekli koşturarak zamanın hizmetkârı haline geldik.
items.en: Some thinkers say we became servants of time, forever rushing.

items.q: What is the main idea of the final paragraph?

Everyone should throw away their clocks

items.en: The final paragraph's main idea is that clocks brought order but also a sense that time is running out.

articles.title: The Toughest Animal on Earth
articles.body:
It is smaller than a grain of sand, lives in the moss on garden walls, and may be the most indestructible creature ever studied. The tardigrade, sometimes called the water bear, looks almost comical under a microscope, plodding along on eight stubby legs. Yet this tiny animal can survive conditions that would kill almost anything else.

When its watery home dries out, the tardigrade performs an extraordinary trick. It pulls in its legs, expels most of the water from its body, and curls into a dry, lifeless-looking ball. In this state, its inner workings almost completely stop. It can remain this way for years, and then, when water returns, it slowly comes back to life as though nothing had happened.

In this dried-out form, tardigrades have endured tests that sound like science fiction. They have survived being frozen to nearly the coldness of outer space, heated above the boiling point of water, and even exposed to the vacuum and radiation of space itself. Few, if any, other animals could withstand such extremes.

Scientists are fascinated not just by the toughness of these creatures but by how they achieve it. Understanding the special substances that protect a tardigrade's cells could one day help us store medicines without refrigeration, or protect human tissue from damage. The humble water bear, it turns out, may have lessons to teach us all.

items.q: What does a tardigrade do when its home dries out?
opts: It curls into a dry ball and nearly stops functioning
It swims to a new pond
items.tr: Su kuruyunca tardigrad kuru bir top haline gelir ve işlevleri neredeyse durur.
items.en: It curls into a dry ball and its inner workings almost completely stop.

items.q: What happens when water returns to a dried tardigrade?
opts: It slowly comes back to life
items.tr: Su geri geldiğinde tardigrad yavaşça yeniden canlanır.
items.en: When water returns, it slowly comes back to life.

items.q: Which extreme condition have tardigrades survived?
opts: The vacuum and radiation of space
items.tr: Tardigradlar uzayın boşluğu ve radyasyonu gibi koşullara dayanmıştır.
items.en: Tardigrades have survived the vacuum and radiation of space.

items.q: Why are scientists interested in how tardigrades survive?
opts: It could help store medicines without refrigeration
items.tr: Bilim insanları, bunun ilaçları soğutmadan saklamaya yardımcı olabileceği için ilgileniyor.
items.en: Understanding it could help store medicines without refrigeration.

items.q: What is the writer's tone towards the tardigrade?
items.tr: Yazarın tardigrada karşı tutumu hayranlık ve merak doludur.
items.en: The writer's tone is admiring and curious.

articles.title: More Than a Room of Books
articles.body:
Ask most people what a library is for, and they will say borrowing books. That answer was never quite complete, and today it is more incomplete than ever. The modern public library has quietly become one of the most useful, and most underrated, spaces in any town.

Libraries have always offered something rare: a warm, quiet place that anyone may enter without being asked to buy a thing. For a student with no quiet room at home, a job-seeker who needs the internet, or an older person living alone, this open door can matter enormously. In a world where most public spaces expect us to spend money, the library asks for nothing.

Many libraries now lend far more than books. Visitors can borrow tools, musical instruments, or even seeds for their gardens. They run classes in everything from computer skills to local history, and they offer a meeting place for clubs and community groups. For new arrivals to a country, the library is often the first place to find help in their own language.

None of this means that books no longer matter; they remain at the heart of what a library is. But it does mean that those who measure a library only by the number of books it lends are missing the point. A good library lends opportunity, and that is far harder to count.

items.q: What does the writer say is special about libraries?
opts: Anyone may enter without being asked to buy anything
items.tr: Kütüphanelerin özelliği, kimsenin bir şey satın alması beklenmeden girebilmesidir.
items.en: Anyone may enter a library without being asked to buy anything.

items.q: Who is given as an example of someone the open door helps?
opts: A job-seeker who needs the internet
items.tr: Açık kapının yardımcı olduğu örneklerden biri, internete ihtiyaç duyan bir iş arayandır.
items.en: A job-seeker who needs the internet is given as an example.

items.q: What can visitors borrow from many modern libraries besides books?
items.tr: Birçok modern kütüphaneden kitap dışında alet, çalgı ya da tohum ödünç alınabilir.
items.en: Visitors can borrow tools, instruments, or seeds besides books.

items.q: What does the writer mean by 'a good library lends opportunity'?
opts: A library's value goes beyond the number of books lent
items.tr: Bu ifade, bir kütüphanenin değerinin ödünç verdiği kitap sayısının ötesine geçtiğini anlatır.
items.en: It means a library's value goes beyond the number of books it lends.

items.q: What does the writer think of judging libraries only by book numbers?
items.tr: Yazara göre kütüphaneleri yalnızca kitap sayısıyla değerlendirmek konuyu kaçırmaktır.
items.en: The writer thinks judging libraries only by book numbers misses the point.

articles.title: The Clock Inside Us
articles.body:
Hidden deep within the brain lies a tiny cluster of cells that acts like a master clock, quietly setting the rhythm of nearly everything our bodies do. This internal clock, known as the circadian system, runs on a cycle of roughly twenty-four hours, telling us when to feel awake, when to grow sleepy, and even when to feel hungry.

Left entirely alone, this clock would drift slightly out of step with the real day. To keep it accurate, the body relies on signals from the outside world, the most powerful of which is light. When morning light reaches the eyes, it tells the brain that the day has begun, helping the inner clock to reset itself and stay in time with the sun.

Problems arise when our behaviour and our inner clock fall out of agreement. Travelling quickly across time zones produces the familiar misery of jet lag. Working through the night, or staring at bright screens long after dark, can confuse the system in similar ways, leaving people tired during the day and wide awake at night.

Researchers increasingly believe that a disturbed clock is not merely unpleasant but harmful, linked to poor concentration and a range of health problems. The good news is that the same clock that is so easily upset can also be gently guided. By seeking out daylight in the morning and dimming our screens at night, we can help our inner clock do the job it has been doing for millions of years.

items.q: What does the circadian system do?
opts: It sets the rhythm of nearly everything the body does
items.tr: Sirkadiyen sistem, bedenin yaptığı neredeyse her şeyin ritmini ayarlar.
items.en: The circadian system sets the rhythm of nearly everything the body does.

items.q: What is the most powerful signal that keeps the inner clock accurate?

articles.title: The Material That Built the Modern World
articles.body:
Look around almost any city and you will see it everywhere: in pavements, bridges, tunnels, and towers. Concrete is so common that we barely notice it, yet it is the most widely used building material on Earth after water. Its story stretches back thousands of years and reaches right into the problems of our own age.

The secret of concrete is surprisingly simple. When a grey powder called cement is mixed with water, sand, and stones, a chemical reaction begins that turns the soft, wet mixture into something as hard as rock. Because it can be poured into almost any shape before it sets, concrete lets builders create forms that would be impossible with cut stone alone.

The ancient Romans were masters of this material, and some of their concrete structures still stand after two thousand years. Strangely, the knowledge of how to make such durable concrete was largely lost for centuries, and only rediscovered and improved in the modern age. Today, enormous quantities are produced every year to house a growing and increasingly urban population.

This success comes at a cost. Making cement releases large amounts of carbon dioxide, so concrete is now a significant contributor to climate change. Scientists are racing to develop greener versions, and even concrete that can repair its own cracks. The challenge is to keep the benefits of this remarkable material while reducing the harm it does to the planet.

items.en: Concrete is the most widely used building material after water.

opts: It can be poured into almost any shape before it sets
items.tr: Beton, sertleşmeden önce neredeyse her şekle dökülebildiği için çok kullanışlıdır.
items.en: It can be poured into almost any shape before it sets.

articles.title: Why We Tell Stories
articles.body:
Every known human society, from the largest city to the smallest village, tells stories. Long before writing existed, people sat around fires and shared tales of heroes, animals, and faraway places. Storytelling is so old and so universal that many scientists believe it is a basic part of being human.

But why do we do it? One reason is that stories help us learn. A story about a child who wanders too far and meets danger teaches a lesson far more powerfully than a simple warning ever could. Through stories, each generation passes on what it has learned about the world.

Stories also bring people together. When we share a tale, we share feelings, and for a short time we see the world through someone else's eyes. This may help explain why we care so deeply about characters who do not even exist. A good story can make us laugh, cry, or hold our breath, all while we sit perfectly still.

Today we tell stories in new ways, through films, games, and screens of every kind, but the basic activity has not changed. We are still doing what our ancestors did around the fire: making sense of our lives by turning them into stories, and sharing those stories with one another.

articles.title: When a Newcomer Takes Over
articles.body:
Sometimes a plant or animal is carried, by accident or on purpose, to a part of the world where it has never lived before. Most such travellers simply fail to survive. A few, however, find their new home so welcoming that they spread out of control, and these are what scientists call invasive species.

The danger comes from the absence of limits. In its original home, a species is held in check by the predators, diseases, and competitors it evolved alongside. Carried to a new land without any of these, it may multiply with astonishing speed, crowding out native plants and animals that have no defence against it.

The results can be severe. A single introduced fish can empty a lake of the species that lived there for thousands of years. An imported insect can destroy forests across an entire continent. Beyond the harm to nature, invasive species cost the world's economies enormous sums each year in lost crops and damaged waterways.

Dealing with them is notoriously difficult. Once a species is firmly established, removing it completely is often impossible, and the methods used can themselves cause harm. For this reason, experts stress that prevention is far cheaper and more effective than cure. Stopping a newcomer before it arrives is, almost always, the wisest course of all.

items.en: An invasive species spreads out of control in a new home.

opts: It has no predators or competitors in the new land
items.tr: İstilacı tür, yeni topraklarda kendisini sınırlayan avcı veya rakibi olmadığı için hızla çoğalır.
items.en: It multiplies fast because it has no predators or competitors in the new land.

items.en: Once established, removing them completely is often impossible.

listening.title: A short lecture on orbits
listening.script: In today's session we'll look briefly at why the planets in our solar system stay in orbit, rather than flying off into space or falling into the Sun. The key idea is gravity. Every object with mass pulls on every other object, and the Sun, being by far the most massive thing in our neighbourhood, exerts an enormous pull on the planets. You might then ask why the planets don't simply crash into it. The answer is that they are also moving sideways, very fast. The result is a kind of balance: a planet is constantly falling toward the Sun, but it is travelling forward so quickly that it keeps missing. We call this stable, curving path an orbit, and the same principle keeps the Moon circling the Earth.

listening.title: A talk about healthy eating
listening.script: Welcome, everyone. Today I want to clear up a common misunderstanding about healthy eating. Many people believe that the secret is simply to eat less of everything, but that approach often fails, and here's why. When we cut our food too sharply, the body responds by slowing down and making us feel hungry, so most people give up within a few weeks. A better strategy is not to eat less, but to eat differently. Try filling half your plate with vegetables, choosing whole grains over white bread, and keeping sugary drinks for special occasions rather than every day. Notice that none of this asks you to go hungry. Another point worth remembering is that no single food is magic, and no single food is poison. It's the overall pattern, repeated over months and years, that shapes your health, not what you happen to eat on any one afternoon. So be patient with yourself, make small changes you can keep, and let those changes add up.

listening.title: A lesson on the water cycle
listening.script: In today's lesson, we'll follow a single drop of water on its endless journey around our planet. Let's start in the ocean. When the sun heats the surface of the sea, water turns into an invisible gas called water vapour and rises into the air. This process is known as evaporation. As the vapour climbs higher, the air around it grows colder, and the vapour cools and gathers into tiny droplets, forming the clouds we see overhead. We call this stage condensation. When those droplets join together and become heavy enough, they fall back to the ground as rain or, in colder places, as snow. Some of this water soaks into the soil and is taken up by plants; some flows into rivers that carry it, eventually, all the way back to the sea. And then the whole cycle begins again. The important thing to remember is that no new water is created or destroyed. The very same water has been moving around the Earth for billions of years.

listening.title: A first-aid radio segment
listening.script: And now for our weekly health segment. Today we're talking about a simple skill that everyone should know: what to do if someone burns their hand in the kitchen. The first and most important step is to cool the burn under cool running water for at least twenty minutes. I'll say that again, because people often stop too soon: twenty minutes of cool, not freezing, running water. While you do this, gently remove any rings or watches from the area before it begins to swell. Whatever you do, don't put ice directly on the skin, and don't use butter or toothpaste, despite what you may have heard, as these can make things worse. After cooling, cover the burn loosely with clean kitchen film or a clean plastic bag. For anything larger than the size of your hand, or any burn on the face, always seek medical help straight away. A few calm minutes of the right action can make a real difference to how well a burn heals.

grammar.title: Conditionals (Type 0-1-2-3)
grammar.exp: Type 0 genel gerçek: If + present, present (If you heat ice, it melts). Type 1 gerçekçi gelecek: If + present, will + V1 (If it rains, we'll stay in). Type 2 hayali şimdi/gelecek: If + past, would + V1 (If I had time, I would help). Type 3 geçmişe pişmanlık: If + had + V3, would have + V3. Tuzak: 'if' cümleciğinde 'will' kullanma; Type 2'de resmî dilde tüm öznelerle 'were' (If I were you).

If I ___ you, I would apologise.
If she had studied, she ___ the exam.
We would travel more if we ___ more money.
If you heat ice, it ___.
I'll call you if I ___ time.

grammar.title: The Passive Voice
grammar.exp: Edilgen yapı: be + V3 (fiilin üçüncü hali). Eylemi yapan bilinmiyor ya da önemsizse kullanılır: The bridge was built in 1990. 'be' fiili zamana göre değişir (is made / was made / will be made / has been made). Eylemi yapan önemliyse 'by' ile verilir. Tuzak: geçişsiz fiiller (happen, arrive, exist) edilgen yapılamaz.

items.q: The letter ___ yesterday.
English ___ all over the world.
The bridge ___ in 1905.
This room ___ every day.
A new hospital ___ next year.
The cake ___ by my sister.

grammar.title: Relative Clauses
grammar.exp: who (insan), which (nesne/hayvan), that (her ikisi, sadece defining), where (yer), whose (iyelik). Defining clause virgülsüzdür ve cümle için gereklidir; non-defining clause virgüllüdür ve ek bilgi verir. Tuzak: non-defining (virgüllü) clause'da 'that' kullanılmaz; virgülden sonra 'which' veya 'who' gelir.

items.q: The woman ___ lives next door is a doctor.
That's the village ___ I grew up.
The book ___ you lent me was great.
My brother, ___ lives in Paris, is a chef.
This is the student ___ project won the prize.
The film ___ we saw last night was boring.

grammar.title: Reported Speech
grammar.exp: Dolaylı anlatımda zaman bir adım geriye kayar: present -> past, will -> would, can -> could, present perfect -> past perfect. Zaman/yer zarfları da değişir (now -> then, tomorrow -> the next day). Tuzak: soruları aktarırken düz cümle dizilişi kullanılır ve evet/hayır sorularında 'if/whether' eklenir (He asked if I was ready).

items.q: She said she ___ tired.
He told me he ___ help the next day.
They asked ___ I was ready.
Tom said he ___ finished his work.
She asked me where I ___.
items.tr: Soru aktarımı düz diziliş + zaman geriye -> lived.

items.q: He said he would come ___.

grammar.title: Gerund and Infinitive
grammar.exp: Bazı fiiller -ing ister (enjoy, avoid, finish, mind), bazıları to + V1 (want, decide, hope, plan). Anlam değiştirenler var: 'stop doing' (bırakmak) ≠ 'stop to do' (yapmak için durmak). Tuzak: edattan (at, of, about, in) sonra daima -ing gelir (good at swimming).

items.q: I enjoy ___ in the sea.
She decided ___ abroad.
He's very good at ___ problems.
On the way home we stopped ___ a coffee.
items.tr: 'stop to do' = yapmak için durmak -> to have.

items.q: Would you mind ___ the door?
They hope ___ the match on Saturday.

grammar.title: Inversion
grammar.exp: Olumsuz veya sınırlayıcı bir zarf cümle başına gelince özne ile yardımcı fiil yer değiştirir (devrik yapı): Never have I seen...; Not only did he..., but...; Hardly had I arrived when... . Tuzak: devrik yapıda soru dizilişi kullanılır (yardımcı fiil + özne); düz dizilişe dönme ve yardımcı fiili (do/did/have) unutma.

items.q: Never ___ such a beautiful view.
items.tr: Olumsuz başlangıç -> devrik: have I seen.

items.q: Not only ___ late, but he also forgot the keys.
Hardly ___ when the phone rang.
items.tr: Hardly ... when -> devrik: had I arrived.

items.q: Seldom ___ such dedication in a student.
No sooner had she left ___ it started to rain.
Only after the meeting ___ the truth.
items.tr: Only after + devrik -> did I learn.

grammar.title: Wish / If only
grammar.exp: Şimdiki gerçeğe karşı istek: wish + past (I wish I knew). Geçmişe pişmanlık: wish + had + V3 (I wish I had studied). Başkasının davranışından şikâyet: wish + would (I wish it would stop raining). 'If only' aynı kalıpları daha vurgulu kullanır. Tuzak: resmî dilde 'I wish I was' yerine 'I wish I were'.

items.q: I wish I ___ how to drive.
She wishes she ___ harder for the exam.
I wish it ___ raining; I want to go out.
If only I ___ taller!
He wishes he ___ that mistake last year.
I wish you ___ so loudly; I can't concentrate.

grammar.title: Articles (a / an / the)
grammar.exp: a/an: ilk kez geçen, tekil sayılabilen isim (a book, an hour). the: belirli, daha önce anılan ya da tek olan (the sun, the book I bought). Sıfır artikel: genel anlamda çoğul ya da sayılamayan isim (Cats are independent). Tuzak: seçim YAZIYA değil SESE göre yapılır: 'an hour' (sessiz h), 'a university' (yu- sesi).

items.q: She is ___ honest person.
items.tr: 'honest' sessiz h, ünlü sesle başlar -> an.

items.q: I looked up at ___ moon last night.
He plays ___ guitar very well.
___ tigers are dangerous animals.
We waited for ___ hour.
She wants to be ___ engineer.
items.tr: Ünlü sesle başlayan meslek -> an engineer.

grammar.title: Comparatives and Superlatives
grammar.exp: Kısa sıfat + -er + than (taller than). Uzun sıfat: more + sıfat + than (more expensive than). Eşitlik: as + sıfat + as. Üstünlük: the + -est / the most. Tuzak: çift karşılaştırma yapma ('more taller' yanlış). Düzensizler: good-better-best, bad-worse-worst.

items.q: This box is ___ than that one.
Today is ___ than yesterday.
She is ___ student in the class.
A car is ___ expensive than a bike.
He runs ___ as his brother.
This is ___ film I have ever seen.

grammar.title: Perfect Tenses
grammar.exp: Present perfect: have/has + V3, geçmişte olup şimdiye etkisi süren (I have finished). Past perfect: had + V3, geçmişte başka bir olaydan önce (She had left before I arrived). Future perfect: will have + V3, gelecekte bir andan önce tamamlanacak (By 2030 they will have built it). Tuzak: belirli geçmiş zarfıyla (yesterday, in 2010) present perfect kullanma -> past simple.

items.q: I ___ already finished my homework.
By the time we arrived, the film ___.
items.tr: Geçmişte önce olan -> past perfect 'had started'.

items.q: She ___ here since 2010.
By next June, I ___ my degree.
He ___ his keys, so he couldn't get in.
I ___ that film yesterday.

grammar.title: Quantifiers (much / many / few / little)
grammar.exp: Sayılabilen isimlerle 'many, (a) few, a number of'; sayılamayanlarla 'much, (a) little, an amount of' kullanılır. 'a few/a little' = biraz (olumlu); 'few/little' = neredeyse hiç (olumsuz vurgu). 'some' olumlu cümlede, 'any' olumsuz ve soruda gelir. Tuzak: 'much' çoğunlukla olumsuz/soru cümlesinde kullanılır; olumlu cümlede 'a lot of' tercih edilir.

items.q: How ___ sugar do you take in your coffee?
There are too ___ cars in the city centre.
I have only a ___ minutes, so let's be quick.
She has very ___ patience with lazy people.
Would you like ___ tea?
We didn't have ___ money left after the trip.

grammar.title: Linking Devices (and / but / so / because)
grammar.exp: Bağlaçlar cümleler arasında ilişki kurar: 'and' ekleme, 'but' karşıtlık, 'so' sonuç, 'because' neden, 'although' ödün, 'or' seçenek bildirir. Tuzak: 'because' nedeni, 'so' sonucu gösterir; karıştırma. 'although' ile 'but' aynı cümlede birlikte kullanılmaz.

items.q: It was raining, ___ we stayed at home.
I was tired ___ I had worked all day.
She is rich ___ she is not happy.
___ it was cold, we went swimming.
Would you like tea ___ coffee?
He studied hard, ___ he passed the exam.

grammar.title: Future Perfect (will have done)
grammar.exp: Gelecekte belirli bir andan ÖNCE tamamlanmış olacak eylemler için 'will have + V3' kullanılır: By 2030, they will have finished the bridge. Genellikle 'by + zaman' veya 'by the time ...' ifadeleriyle gelir. Tuzak: 'by the time' yan cümlesinde gelecek değil GENİŞ zaman kullanılır (By the time you arrive, I will have left).

items.q: By next June, I ___ my degree.
items.tr: Gelecekte bir andan önce tamamlanır -> will have finished.

items.q: By the time you ___ home, we will have eaten.
items.tr: 'by the time' yan cümlesi geniş zaman -> get.

items.q: They ___ the report by Friday.
In two hours, the train ___ the city.
items.tr: Belirli andan önce tamamlanır -> will have reached.

items.q: By the end of the year, she ___ here for a decade.
items.tr: Bir noktaya kadar süregelmiş -> will have worked.

items.q: By midnight, they ___ all the tickets.
items.tr: Gece yarısından önce tamamlanmış -> will have sold.

grammar.title: Causatives (have / get something done)
grammar.exp: Bir işi başkasına yaptırmayı anlatmak için 'have/get + nesne + V3' kullanılır: I had my car repaired (arabamı tamir ettirdim). 'get' daha gündelik. Kişiye yaptırma için 'have somebody do' veya 'get somebody to do' kalıbı vardır. Tuzak: 'I repaired my car' kendin yaptın demektir; başkasına yaptırdıysan 'had it repaired' de.

items.q: I'm going to ___ my hair cut tomorrow.
She had the kitchen ___ last month.
We need to get the windows ___.
He had the mechanic ___ the engine.
They got an expert ___ the painting.
items.tr: get somebody to do -> to examine.

items.q: I must have these documents ___ today.

grammar.title: Modals of Deduction (must / might / can't)
grammar.exp: Çıkarım yaparken: kesin olumlu -> 'must' (He must be tired); olası -> 'might/may/could'; kesin olumsuz -> 'can't' (She can't be at home). Geçmiş için 'must have / might have / can't have + V3'. Tuzak: olumsuz kesin çıkarımda 'mustn't' değil 'can't' kullanılır (He can't be the thief).

items.q: The lights are off; they ___ be asleep.
She isn't answering; she ___ be busy.
You ___ be serious! That's impossible.
He ___ have missed the bus; that's why he's late.
They ___ have heard the news yet; they look calm.
Nobody answered. They ___ have gone out.

grammar.title: Noun Clauses (that / wh- / if-whether)
grammar.exp: İsim cümlecikleri özne ya da nesne yerine geçer: I know that he is right. Soru sözcükleriyle gelenlerde DÜZ diziliş kullanılır (I don't know where she lives, 'does she live' değil). Evet/hayır soruları 'if/whether' ile aktarılır. Tuzak: gömülü soruda yardımcı fiil-özne devrik olmaz.

items.q: Do you know ___ the museum opens?
items.tr: Gömülü soru düz diziliş -> when (+ özne + fiil).

items.q: I'm not sure ___ he will come or not.
She told me ___ she was tired.
Can you tell me where ___?
___ he said surprised everyone.
I wonder ___ the test will be difficult.

grammar.title: Participle Clauses
grammar.exp: İki cümleyi kısaltmak için ortaç kullanılır. Etken/eşzamanlı için '-ing' (Opening the door, she smiled = As she opened ...). Edilgen/önce biten için '-ed/V3' (Built in 1900, the house ...). Neden de gösterebilir (Feeling tired, he left). Tuzak: ortacın öznesi ana cümlenin öznesiyle AYNI olmalı; aksi halde 'dangling' hata olur.

items.q: ___ the letter, she began to cry.
items.tr: Etken eşzamanlı -> Reading (= As she read).

items.q: ___ in 1920, the bridge is still in use.
___ tired, he went straight to bed.
The man ___ in the corner is my uncle.
___ by the noise, the baby woke up.
___ what to say, she stayed silent.

grammar.title: Cleft Sentences (It is / What ...)
grammar.exp: Bir ögeyi vurgulamak için cümle ikiye bölünür. 'It + be + vurgulanan + that/who ...' (It was John who broke it). 'What + cümle + be ...' (What I need is a holiday). Tuzak: 'It was ... that' kalıbında vurgulanan nesne de olsa 'that' kullanılır; özneyse 'who' de olabilir.

items.q: ___ John who solved the problem.
___ I really want is some peace and quiet.
items.tr: 'What' yarık cümle -> What I want is ...

items.q: It was in Paris ___ they first met.
___ surprised me was his honesty.
It is the climate ___ attracts tourists here.
What she did ___ call the police immediately.
items.tr: 'What ... was to + V1' kalıbı -> was to.

grammar.title: Mixed Conditionals
grammar.exp: Karma koşul cümleleri farklı zamanları birleştirir. Geçmişteki bir koşulun ŞİMDİKİ sonucu: If + had + V3, would + V1 (If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now). Şimdiki bir durumun GEÇMİŞTEKİ sonucu: If + past, would have + V3 (If I were brave, I would have told her). Tuzak: zaman göstergelerine (now, today / then, yesterday) dikkat ederek doğru yapıyı seç.

items.q: If I had saved money, I ___ rich now.
items.tr: Geçmiş koşul + şimdiki sonuç -> would be.

items.q: If she were more careful, she ___ that mistake yesterday.
items.tr: Şimdiki durum + geçmiş sonuç -> wouldn't have made.

items.q: If he hadn't missed the train, he ___ here by now.
items.tr: Geçmiş koşul + şimdiki sonuç -> would be.

items.q: If I didn't love this job, I ___ it years ago.
items.tr: Şimdiki durum + geçmiş sonuç -> would have left.

items.q: If they had taken the map, they ___ lost now.
items.tr: Geçmiş koşul + şimdiki sonuç -> wouldn't be.

items.q: If she spoke German, she ___ the job in Berlin last month.
items.tr: Şimdiki yeti + geçmiş sonuç -> would have got.

grammar.title: The Subjunctive (suggest / insist that ...)
grammar.exp: Öneri, talep, ısrar bildiren fiil ve sıfatlardan sonra (suggest, insist, demand, recommend, essential, important) 'that' cümleciğinde fiilin YALIN hâli (base form) kullanılır, özne ne olursa olsun: I suggest that he be present. Olumsuzda 'that he not go'. Tuzak: 'he is/goes' değil, kişide bile 'be/go' yalın biçim gelir.

items.q: The teacher insisted that he ___ on time.
It is essential that she ___ the rules.
I recommend that he ___ a doctor.
They demanded that the report ___ ready by noon.
The doctor advised that he ___ not smoke.
It is important that everyone ___ the form.

grammar.title: Verb 'to be' (am / is / are)
grammar.exp:
İngilizcede 'to be' fiili (am / is / are) 'olmak' anlamına gelir; kimlik, durum ve yer bildirir. Özneye göre çekimlenir: I am; you / we / they are; he / she / it is. Konuşmada kısaltmalar yaygındır: I'm, you're, he's. Olumsuzda 'not' eklenir (is not = isn't). Soruda fiil öne alınır: Are you ready?

Örnekler:
• I am a teacher. (Ben bir öğretmenim.)
• She is at home. (O evde.)
• They are very happy. (Onlar çok mutlu.)
• Are you tired? (Yorgun musun?)

Sık tuzaklar: Türkçede 'olmak' çoğu zaman söylenmez ('Ben mutluyum'), ama İngilizcede 'to be' asla düşmez: 'I happy' YANLIŞ, 'I am happy' doğru. Ayrıca özneye doğru biçimi seç: 'He are' değil 'He is'.

items.q: I ___ a student at this school.
She ___ my best friend.
They ___ from Spain.
___ you a doctor?
The cat ___ under the table.
We ___ ready to start.
He ___ not at work today.
My parents ___ very kind.

grammar.title: Present Simple
grammar.exp:
Geniş zaman (Present Simple), alışkanlıkları, tekrarlanan eylemleri ve genel gerçekleri anlatır. Fiil yalın hâlde kullanılır; ama özne 'he / she / it' ise fiile -s (veya -es) eklenir: I work / she works. Olumsuz ve soru için yardımcı fiil 'do / does' gelir ve ana fiil yalın kalır: I don't work; Does he work?

Örnekler:
• I drink tea every morning. (Her sabah çay içerim.)
• She lives in Ankara. (O Ankara'da yaşar.)
• Water boils at 100 degrees. (Su 100 derecede kaynar.)
• Do you like music? (Müzik sever misin?)

Sık tuzaklar: 3. tekil şahısta -s'i unutma: 'She work' YANLIŞ, 'She works' doğru. Soru/olumsuzda -s yardımcı fiile geçer, ana fiile değil: 'Does she works?' YANLIŞ, 'Does she work?' doğru.

items.q: She ___ to school by bus.
I ___ coffee in the morning.
___ he speak English?
They ___ television every evening.
The sun ___ in the east.
We ___ like spicy food.
My brother ___ football on Sundays.
I ___ understand this question.

grammar.title: Present Continuous
grammar.exp:
Şimdiki zaman (Present Continuous), tam şu anda ya da bu günlerde süren eylemleri anlatır. Yapısı: özneye uygun 'to be' (am / is / are) + fiil + -ing. Olumsuzda 'to be' + not; soruda 'to be' öne alınır.

Örnekler:
• I am reading a book now. (Şu an bir kitap okuyorum.)
• She is cooking dinner. (O yemek yapıyor.)
• They are playing outside. (Onlar dışarıda oynuyor.)
• What are you doing? (Ne yapıyorsun?)

Sık tuzaklar: 'to be' fiilini unutma: 'I reading' YANLIŞ, 'I am reading' doğru. Ayrıca 'like, want, know, love' gibi durum fiilleri genellikle -ing almaz: 'I am knowing' YANLIŞ, 'I know' doğru.

items.q: Look! The baby ___ .
items.tr: Şu an süren eylem -> is sleeping.

items.q: I ___ my homework right now.
What ___ you ___ ?
items.tr: Şimdiki zaman sorusu -> are you doing.

items.q: They ___ football at the moment.
She ___ TV; she is studying.
We ___ for the bus now.
He ___ a letter to his friend.
Why ___ you crying?
items.tr: Şimdiki zaman sorusu -> are you crying.

grammar.title: There is / There are
grammar.exp:
Bir şeyin var olduğunu ya da bir yerde bulunduğunu söylemek için 'There is' (tekil) ve 'There are' (çoğul) kullanılır. Sayılamayan isimlerle 'There is' gelir. Olumsuz: There isn't / There aren't. Soru: Is there ...? / Are there ...?

Örnekler:
• There is a book on the table. (Masada bir kitap var.)
• There are three chairs in the room. (Odada üç sandalye var.)
• There isn't any milk. (Hiç süt yok.)
• Are there any questions? (Herhangi bir soru var mı?)

Sık tuzaklar: Fiili isme göre seç: 'There is two cats' YANLIŞ, 'There are two cats' doğru. Soru ve olumsuzda çoğunlukla 'any' kullanılır: 'Is there any bread?' Türkçedeki 'var' düşmez, İngilizcede 'there is/are' gereklidir.

items.q: ___ a big park near my house.
___ many people at the party.
___ any sugar in the coffee?
There ___ four seasons in a year.
There ___ any bread left.
___ there any apples in the fridge?
There ___ a problem with the car.
There ___ two banks on this street.

grammar.title: Prepositions of Place (in / on / at / under)
grammar.exp:
Yer edatları bir şeyin nerede olduğunu gösterir. 'in' kapalı/çevrili alan (in the box, in London), 'on' yüzey (on the table, on the wall), 'at' nokta/belirli yer (at the door, at the bus stop), 'under' altında, 'next to / between / behind / in front of' konum bildirir.

Örnekler:
• The keys are in my bag. (Anahtarlar çantamda.)
• The picture is on the wall. (Resim duvarda.)
• I'm waiting at the bus stop. (Otobüs durağında bekliyorum.)
• The cat is under the bed. (Kedi yatağın altında.)

Sık tuzaklar: Şehir/ülke için 'in' (in Turkey), belirli nokta için 'at' (at the airport). 'on' yüzeyle ilgilidir: 'on the table' (masanın üstünde), 'in the table' değil. Türkçedeki '-de/-da' üç ayrı edata karşılık gelebilir; bağlama bak.

items.q: The milk is ___ the fridge.
Your phone is ___ the desk.
I'll meet you ___ the station.
The ball rolled ___ the sofa.
She lives ___ Istanbul.
The bank is ___ the post office and the café.
There is a lamp ___ the table.
Wait for me ___ the door.

grammar.title: Can / Can't (Ability & Permission)
grammar.exp:
'can' yeteneği ('yapabilmek'), olasılığı ve izni anlatan bir kip fiilidir. Ardından fiilin yalın hâli gelir (can + V1); özneye göre değişmez. Olumsuzu 'cannot / can't'. Soruda 'can' öne alınır: Can you swim?

Örnekler:
• I can swim very well. (Çok iyi yüzebilirim.)
• She can't drive a car. (O araba kullanamaz.)
• Can you help me, please? (Bana yardım edebilir misin?)
• We can meet tomorrow. (Yarın buluşabiliriz.)

Sık tuzaklar: 'can'den sonra 'to' kullanma: 'I can to swim' YANLIŞ, 'I can swim' doğru. Fiile -s ekleme: 'She cans' YANLIŞ, 'She can' doğru. Ana fiil daima yalın: 'can swims' değil 'can swim'.

items.q: I ___ play the guitar.
___ you speak French?
She ___ swim; she's afraid of water.
We can ___ tomorrow if you're free.
___ I open the window, please?
He ___ ride a bike now.
Birds ___ fly, but they can't talk.
I'm sorry, I ___ come to your party.

grammar.title: Past Simple
grammar.exp:
Geçmiş zaman (Past Simple), geçmişte başlayıp biten eylemleri anlatır. Düzenli fiillere -ed eklenir (work → worked); düzensiz fiillerin özel biçimi vardır (go → went, see → saw). Olumsuz ve soruda yardımcı fiil 'did' kullanılır ve ana fiil YALIN hâle döner: I didn't go; Did you see?

Örnekler:
• I visited my grandmother yesterday. (Dün büyükannemi ziyaret ettim.)
• She went to Paris last year. (Geçen yıl Paris'e gitti.)
• We didn't watch the film. (Filmi izlemedik.)
• Did they arrive on time? (Zamanında geldiler mi?)

Sık tuzaklar: 'did' varken ana fiil geçmiş hâlde olmaz: 'Did you went?' YANLIŞ, 'Did you go?' doğru. Düzensiz fiilleri ezberle: 'goed' değil 'went'.

items.q: We ___ a great film last night.
She ___ to London in 2019.
___ you enjoy the party?
They ___ come to the meeting.
I ___ a strange noise last night.
Did she ___ the email?
He ___ his keys at home yesterday.
We ___ dinner at eight o'clock.

grammar.title: Past Continuous
grammar.exp:
Sürekli geçmiş zaman (Past Continuous), geçmişte belirli bir anda süregelen eylemi anlatır. Yapısı: was / were + fiil + -ing. Çoğu zaman Past Simple ile birlikte kullanılır: uzun eylem -ing'li, onu kesen kısa eylem geçmiş yalın hâlde ('when' ile) gelir.

Örnekler:
• I was reading when the phone rang. (Telefon çaldığında okuyordum.)
• They were playing in the garden. (Bahçede oynuyorlardı.)
• What were you doing at ten? (Saat onda ne yapıyordun?)
• While she was cooking, he arrived. (O yemek yaparken adam geldi.)

Sık tuzaklar: was/were seçimini özneye göre yap: I/he/she/it → was, you/we/they → were. Kesen kısa eylem Past Simple olur: 'when the phone was ringing I answered' yerine 'when the phone rang, I answered'.

items.q: I ___ TV when you called.
They ___ football at six o'clock.
While she ___ , the lights went out.
What ___ you doing at midnight?
He ___ when the accident happened.
We ___ dinner when they arrived.
The sun ___ , so we went out.
I ___ not sleeping at that time.

grammar.title: Future: will & be going to
grammar.exp:
Gelecekten söz etmenin iki yaygın yolu vardır. 'will + V1' anlık kararları, tahminleri ve söz vermeleri anlatır. 'be going to + V1' önceden yapılmış planları ve kanıta dayalı tahminleri anlatır.

Örnekler:
• I'll help you with your bags. (Çantalarına yardım ederim. — anlık karar)
• I'm going to visit Rome next month. (Gelecek ay Roma'yı ziyaret edeceğim. — plan)
• It will rain tomorrow. (Yarın yağmur yağacak. — tahmin)
• Look at those clouds! It's going to rain. (Şu bulutlara bak! Yağmur yağacak. — kanıt var)

Sık tuzaklar: Konuşurken kurulan karar için 'going to' yerine 'will' kullan. Planlanmış şeyler için 'will' yerine 'be going to' daha doğaldır. 'be going to'da 'be' fiilini unutma: 'I going to' YANLIŞ, 'I am going to' doğru.

items.q: The phone is ringing. I ___ answer it.
We ___ move to a new house next year.
items.tr: Önceden yapılmış plan -> are going to.

items.q: Look at the sky! It ___ snow.
items.tr: Kanıta dayalı tahmin -> is going to.

items.q: Don't worry, I ___ tell anyone.
She ___ study medicine; she has decided.
I think our team ___ win the match.
They ___ get married in June.
Maybe I ___ call you later.

grammar.title: Countable & Uncountable Nouns
grammar.exp:
Sayılabilen isimler (countable) tek tek sayılabilir ve çoğul alır: a book / two books. Sayılamayan isimler (uncountable) sayılmaz ve çoğul almaz: water, money, information, advice, bread. Sayılamayanlarla 'a/an' kullanılmaz; miktar için 'some, any, a lot of, a little/much' gelir; sayılabilenlerle 'many, a few' kullanılır.

Örnekler:
• I need some information. (Biraz bilgiye ihtiyacım var.)
• She gave me good advice. (Bana iyi öğüt verdi.)
• There are many books here. (Burada çok kitap var.)
• How much money do you have? (Ne kadar paran var?)

Sık tuzaklar: 'informations, advices, moneys' YANLIŞTIR — bu isimler çoğul almaz. Saymak için 'a piece of' kullan: 'a piece of advice'. 'many' sayılabilenlerle, 'much' sayılamayanlarla gelir.

items.q: I'd like some ___ , please.
How ___ water do you drink daily?
She bought three ___ at the market.
There are too ___ cars in the city.
Can you give me some ___ ?
We only have a ___ eggs left.
He doesn't have ___ money.
I need to buy some ___ .

grammar.title: Adverbs of Frequency
grammar.exp:
Sıklık zarfları bir eylemin ne sıklıkla yapıldığını gösterir: always (%100), usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never (%0). Cümlede yeri önemlidir: ana fiilden ÖNCE, ama 'to be' fiilinden SONRA gelir.

Örnekler:
• I always brush my teeth at night. (Geceleri hep dişlerimi fırçalarım.)
• She is usually late. (O genellikle geç kalır.) — 'be'den sonra
• We sometimes eat out. (Bazen dışarıda yeriz.)
• He never drinks coffee. (O hiç kahve içmez.)

Sık tuzaklar: Zarfı 'be' fiilinden sonra koy: 'She always is late' YANLIŞ, 'She is always late' doğru. 'never' zaten olumsuzdur, ikinci olumsuz ekleme: 'I don't never' YANLIŞ, 'I never' doğru. 'sometimes' cümle başında da olabilir.

items.q: I ___ eat breakfast before work.
She is ___ friendly to everyone.
We ___ go to the cinema.
He ___ drinks alcohol.
They are ___ at home in the evening.
I ___ watch horror films.
My teacher is ___ angry.
___ , we visit our grandparents.

grammar.title: Prepositions of Time (at / on / in)
grammar.exp:
Zaman edatları ne zamanı belirtir. 'at' saat ve belirli anlar için (at 7 o'clock, at night, at the weekend), 'on' gün ve tarihler için (on Monday, on 5th May), 'in' ay, mevsim, yıl ve uzun dönemler için (in July, in summer, in 2020, in the morning).

Örnekler:
• The meeting is at three o'clock. (Toplantı saat üçte.)
• I was born on 12th March. (12 Mart'ta doğdum.)
• We travel in the summer. (Yazın seyahat ederiz.)
• She wakes up early in the morning. (Sabahları erken kalkar.)

Sık tuzaklar: 'in the morning/afternoon/evening' ama 'AT night'. Günlerle 'on', saatlerle 'at' kullan: 'in Monday' YANLIŞ, 'on Monday' doğru. 'next / last / every' ile edat kullanılmaz: 'in next week' değil 'next week'.

items.q: The train leaves ___ 9 o'clock.
My birthday is ___ October.
We have a test ___ Friday.
It gets cold ___ winter.
I don't work ___ night.
She was born ___ 2005.
Let's meet ___ Saturday morning.
The shop opens early ___ the morning.

grammar.title: Possessives ('s and possessive pronouns)
grammar.exp:
Sahiplik göstermenin birkaç yolu vardır. İnsanlar/canlılar için ismin sonuna 's eklenir (Ana's book). Çoğul isimlerde yalnızca kesme işareti gelir (the students' room). İyelik sıfatları isimden önce gelir: my, your, his, her, its, our, their. İyelik zamirleri tek başına kullanılır: mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs.

Örnekler:
• This is Tom's car. (Bu Tom'un arabası.)
• The girls' school is new. (Kızların okulu yeni.)
• Is this your bag? — No, it's hers. (Bu senin çantan mı? — Hayır, onunki.)
• Their house is bigger than ours. (Onların evi bizimkinden büyük.)

Sık tuzaklar: İyelik zamirinden sonra isim gelmez: 'This is mine book' YANLIŞ, 'This is my book' ya da 'This is mine' doğru. 'its' (iyelik) ile 'it's' (it is) karıştırılır.

items.q: This is ___ pencil, not yours.
That bag isn't mine; it's ___ .
I met ___ sister yesterday.
The ___ toys are everywhere.
Is this book ___ ?
The dog wagged ___ tail.
This house is ___ ; we bought it last year.
The ___ room is on the left.

grammar.title: 'should' for Advice
grammar.exp:
'should' bir öneri ya da tavsiye vermek için kullanılan kip fiilidir ('-meli/-malı'). Ardından fiilin yalın hâli gelir (should + V1), özneye göre değişmez. Olumsuzu 'shouldn't' (yapmaman iyi olur). Soruda öne alınır: Should I ...?

Örnekler:
• You should see a doctor. (Bir doktora görünmelisin.)
• He shouldn't eat so much sugar. (O kadar çok şeker yememeli.)
• Should I call her now? (Onu şimdi aramalı mıyım?)
• We should leave early to avoid traffic. (Trafiğe yakalanmamak için erken çıkmalıyız.)

Sık tuzaklar: 'should'dan sonra 'to' kullanma: 'You should to rest' YANLIŞ, 'You should rest' doğru. Fiile -s ekleme: 'She should goes' değil 'She should go'. 'should' zorunluluk değil öneridir; kesin zorunluluk için 'must / have to' kullanılır.

items.q: You look tired. You ___ rest.
He ___ smoke; it's bad for him.
___ I bring an umbrella?
We should ___ early tomorrow.
She ___ study more for the exam.
You ___ tell lies to your friends.
They ___ be more careful with money.
What ___ I do about this problem?

grammar.title: Present Perfect vs Past Simple
grammar.exp:
Past Simple (V2) geçmişte BİTMİŞ, zamanı belli eylemleri anlatır (yesterday, in 2010, last week). Present Perfect (have/has + V3) ise geçmişte olan ama şimdiyle bağı olan, zamanı belirsiz eylemleri anlatır; deneyim (ever/never), yeni bitmiş (just), süregelen durum (for/since) için kullanılır.

Örnekler:
• I saw her yesterday. (Onu dün gördüm. — belirli geçmiş)
• I have seen that film three times. (O filmi üç kez izledim. — deneyim)
• She has lived here since 2015. (2015'ten beri burada yaşıyor. — süregelen)
• Have you ever been to Rome? (Hiç Roma'ya gittin mi?)

Sık tuzaklar: Belirli geçmiş zaman zarfıyla present perfect kullanma: 'I have seen her yesterday' YANLIŞ, 'I saw her yesterday' doğru. 'for' süre (for two years), 'since' başlangıç noktası (since Monday) ile gelir.

items.q: I ___ my keys. I can't find them anywhere.
She ___ to Paris last summer.
We ___ here since 2010.
___ you ever eaten sushi?
He ___ his homework two hours ago.
They ___ just arrived at the airport.
I ___ this book for three days.
When ___ you buy your car?

grammar.title: Past Perfect (had done)
grammar.exp:
Past Perfect (had + V3), geçmişteki BİR olaydan DAHA ÖNCE tamamlanmış başka bir eylemi anlatır; iki geçmiş olayın sırasını netleştirir. Genellikle 'before, after, when, by the time' ile kullanılır. Önce olan eylem past perfect, sonra olan past simple biçimindedir.

Örnekler:
• When I arrived, the train had already left. (Vardığımda tren çoktan kalkmıştı.)
• She had finished dinner before he came. (O gelmeden önce yemeğini bitirmişti.)
• They were tired because they had walked all day. (Bütün gün yürüdükleri için yorgundular.)
• By the time we got there, the shop had closed. (Oraya vardığımızda dükkân kapanmıştı.)

Sık tuzaklar: Sadece tek bir geçmiş olay varsa past perfect gereksizdir; past simple yeterlidir. 'had'i tüm öznelerle kullan (I/he/they had). Sıra açıksa (and, then) genelde past simple tercih edilir.

items.q: The film ___ before we arrived.
She was upset because she ___ the exam.
items.tr: Daha önce olan neden -> had failed.

items.q: By the time I called, he ___ .
items.tr: 'By the time' + önce biten -> had left.

items.q: After they ___ lunch, they went out.
I couldn't enter because I ___ my key.
When we got home, someone ___ the window.
They had never ___ snow before that trip.
The ground was wet; it ___ during the night.

grammar.title: 'used to' for Past Habits
grammar.exp:
'used to + V1', geçmişte düzenli olan ama ARTIK OLMAYAN alışkanlıkları ve durumları anlatır. Olumsuz ve soruda 'did' devreye girer ve 'use to' biçimi (d'siz) kullanılır: didn't use to, Did you use to ...?

Örnekler:
• I used to play football every weekend. (Eskiden her hafta sonu futbol oynardım.)
• She used to have long hair. (Onun eskiden uzun saçı vardı.)
• We didn't use to eat out much. (Eskiden pek dışarıda yemezdik.)
• Did you use to live in the city? (Eskiden şehirde mi yaşardın?)

Sık tuzaklar: Olumsuz/soruda ikinci 'd'yi düşür: 'didn't used to' YANLIŞ, 'didn't use to' doğru. Şu anki alışkanlık için 'used to' kullanılmaz; onun yerine geniş zaman ve sıklık zarfı (usually) gelir. 'be used to + -ing' (alışkın olmak) farklı bir yapıdır.

items.q: I ___ smoke, but I stopped years ago.
She ___ have a dog when she was young.
We didn't ___ travel much.
___ you use to walk to school?
There ___ be a cinema here.
items.tr: Geçmişte vardı, artık yok -> used to.

items.q: He didn't use ___ like vegetables.
They ___ live in a small village.
I used ___ be afraid of the dark.

grammar.title: Present Perfect Continuous (have been doing)
grammar.exp:
Present Perfect Continuous (have/has been + V-ing), geçmişte başlayıp ŞİMDİYE kadar SÜREN ya da yeni durmuş, sonucu görünen eylemleri vurgular. Eylemin ne kadar sürdüğüne odaklanır. 'for, since, all day, lately' ile sık kullanılır.

Örnekler:
• I have been waiting for an hour. (Bir saattir bekliyorum.)
• She has been studying since morning. (Sabahtan beri ders çalışıyor.)
• It has been raining all day. (Bütün gün yağmur yağıyor.)
• You look tired. Have you been running? (Yorgun görünüyorsun. Koşuyor muydun?)

Sık tuzaklar: Durum fiilleri (know, like, be) genelde bu yapıyı almaz. Tamamlanan MİKTAR/sonuç için Present Perfect (have done) daha uygundur: 'I have read three books' (kaç tane) vs 'I have been reading' (ne kadar süre). 'been' fiilini unutma.

items.q: I ___ for you since two o'clock.
items.tr: Süregelen, süre vurgusu -> have been waiting.

items.q: She has ___ studying all afternoon.
They have been ___ in the garden.
How long ___ you been learning English?
It ___ raining since morning.
He's tired because he ___ running.
We ___ been trying to call you.
My eyes hurt; I ___ reading for hours.
items.tr: Sonucu görünen süregelen eylem -> have been.

grammar.title: Question Tags
grammar.exp:
Eklenti sorular (question tags) bir cümlenin sonuna eklenen kısa sorulardır; onay almak ya da teyit etmek için kullanılır. Kural: olumlu cümle → olumsuz tag, olumsuz cümle → olumlu tag. Cümledeki yardımcı fiil (veya 'be') tag'de tekrarlanır; yardımcı yoksa do/does/did kullanılır. Özne zamire dönüşür.

Örnekler:
• You are coming, aren't you? (Geliyorsun, değil mi?)
• She can swim, can't she? (O yüzebilir, değil mi?)
• They don't like it, do they? (Onlar bunu sevmiyor, değil mi?)
• He went home, didn't he? (Eve gitti, değil mi?)

Sık tuzaklar: Olumlu-olumsuz dengesini kur: 'You are ready, are you?' genelde YANLIŞ; 'aren't you?' doğru. 'I am' için tag 'aren't I?' olur. 'Let's' → shall we?; emir → will you?

items.q: You're from Turkey, ___ ?
items.tr: Olumlu cümle -> olumsuz tag: aren't you.

items.q: She can drive, ___ ?
They don't smoke, ___ ?
items.tr: Olumsuz cümle -> olumlu tag: do they.

items.q: He went out, ___ ?
It isn't cold today, ___ ?
We should leave now, ___ ?
You haven't eaten, ___ ?
Let's go for a walk, ___ ?

writing.prompt: Write a formal email to a company about a product that arrived damaged. Explain the problem and say what you want them to do.
writing.tips: Resmî dil kullan (Dear Sir/Madam). Sorunu net anlat, sipariş bilgisini ver, açık bir talep (iade/değişim) ekle, nazik kapat.
writing.structure: Selamlama -> sorun + sipariş detayı -> net talep -> kapanış (I look forward to...).

writing.prompt: Write an informal email to a friend inviting them to spend the weekend at your house. Suggest some activities and explain how to get there.
writing.tips: Samimi bir dil kullan (Hi / Hey). Davetini açıkça yap, birlikte yapabileceğiniz birkaç etkinlik öner, kısa bir yol tarifi ekle ve neşeli bir kapanışla bitir (Can't wait to see you!).
writing.structure: Selamlama -> davet -> etkinlik önerileri -> yol tarifi -> sıcak kapanış.

writing.prompt: Write a formal cover letter applying for a summer internship at an international company. Explain your skills and why you would be a suitable candidate.
writing.tips: Resmî dil kullan (Dear Hiring Manager). Hangi pozisyona başvurduğunu belirt, ilgili beceri ve deneyimlerini somut örneklerle göster, motivasyonunu açıkla ve görüşme talebiyle kapat.
writing.structure: Selamlama -> başvurulan pozisyon -> beceri ve deneyim -> motivasyon -> görüşme talebi + resmî kapanış.

writing.prompt: Write a short story that begins with this sentence: 'When I opened the door, I knew something was wrong.'
writing.tips: Verilen cümleyle başla. Olayları zaman sırasıyla anlat (first, then, suddenly, finally) ve geçmiş zaman kullan. Kısa da olsa bir gerilim/doruk nokta ve net bir sonuç ekle.
writing.structure: Açılış cümlesi -> olayların gelişimi -> doruk nokta -> sonuç.

writing.prompt: Write a review of a film you have seen recently or a restaurant you have visited. Describe it and say whether you would recommend it.
writing.tips: Neyi incelediğini kısaca tanıt, olumlu ve olumsuz yönleri dengeli biçimde ver, kişisel görüşünü gerekçelendir ve net bir tavsiyeyle bitir (öneririm / önermem).
writing.structure: Tanıtım -> olumlu yönler -> olumsuz yönler -> genel değerlendirme + tavsiye.

writing.prompt: Some people think social media brings people closer together, while others believe it makes us more isolated. What is your opinion?
